summary: A small landlocked country in the northeast of the Italian peninsula, completely surrounded by Italy; according to tradition it was founded in AD 301 and is regarded as the oldest surviving republic in the world.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: According to tradition, San Marino was founded in 301 by Saint Marinus, a stonemason from the island of Rab in Dalmatia, who came to live as a hermit on Mount Titano to escape the Roman emperor Diocletian's persecution of Christians. San Marino has therefore been inseparable from Catholicism since its founding; the country's name comes from this saint, and the Feast of San Marino on 3 September each year is the national day. Having long been in the Catholic environment of Italy, Catholicism has always been the faith of the great majority.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: As in Italy, postwar economic development, the spread of education and secularization have led some people to no longer identify with religion. The Constitution of San Marino guarantees freedom of religion, but Catholicism still holds a central place in culture, festivals and state ceremonies, and society as a whole is less secularized than the large countries of Western Europe, so the proportion of non-religious people is not high.

ranking.name: Others
ranking.description: Other religions include small numbers of Protestants, Jehovah's Witnesses and other faiths, whose followers are mainly foreign residents. The Constitution of San Marino guarantees freedom of religion, but because the population is only about thirty thousand, the communities of other religions are very small.

religion.background: According to tradition, San Marino was founded in 301 by the Christian stonemason Saint Marinus and is one of the oldest surviving republics in the world, with Catholicism at its core since its founding. For hundreds of years San Marino has maintained its independence amid the turmoil of the Italian peninsula, and in 1631 the Pope recognized its independent status. During the unification of Italy in the 19th century, San Marino was able to remain independent because it had sheltered Garibaldi. Catholicism is still the main faith of its citizens and is deeply woven into the country's festivals and ceremonies.

ranking.name: Italian
ranking.description: Italian is the official language of San Marino because San Marino is entirely surrounded by Italy and shares a common history and culture with it. After the unification of Italy in the 19th century, standard Italian, based on the Tuscan dialect, spread through education and the media, and San Marino also adopted Italian as its official and educational language.

ranking.name: Romagnol
ranking.description: Romagnol is the local language of the Emilia-Romagna region of northern Italy; it belongs to the Gallo-Italic branch and differs considerably from standard Italian. San Marino lies in the Romagna area, and its inhabitants traditionally spoke Romagnol at home. After standard Italian spread in the 20th century, the number of Romagnol speakers gradually declined and is now concentrated mainly among the elderly.

language.history: In the Roman period Latin was in common use in the San Marino area, and after the Middle Ages it gradually evolved into the Romagnol dialect. For hundreds of years the Sammarinese used Romagnol in daily life, while official documents used Latin and later Italian. After the unification of Italy in the 19th century, standard Italian spread through school education and the media and gradually replaced Romagnol, which today is used mainly among the elderly.

ranking.name: Piadina romagnola
ranking.description: Flour, lard, salt and water are kneaded into a dough, rolled into thin rounds and cooked on a terracotta plate or griddle, then folded in half and filled with prosciutto, squacquerone cheese and arugula.
ranking.history: Piadina is a traditional food of the Romagna region of Italy, with a history that goes back to the Middle Ages; it was originally the everyday bread of farmers because it is quick to make and needs no leavening. In the 19th and 20th centuries the Romagnol poet Pascoli called it the 'national food of the Romagnols'. In San Marino it is the most common street snack and home food, and a must-try for visitors.

ranking.name: Torta Tre Monti (Three Towers wafer cake)
ranking.description: Multiple layers of thin wafers are sandwiched with hazelnut chocolate cream and coated in chocolate on the outside, showing layered stripes when sliced, with a crisp, sweet texture.
ranking.history: The Torta Tre Monti takes its name from the three towers on Mount Titano in San Marino (Guaita, Cesta and Montale), which are national symbols of San Marino and also appear on the flag and coat of arms. The cake was created by a local pastry shop in the first half of the 20th century and is now San Marino's most representative souvenir.

ranking.name: Cappelletti
ranking.description: Pasta dough is wrapped around a cheese or meat filling and pinched into the shape of a little hat, then cooked in clear chicken broth or capon broth, with a clear, savory soup; it is a traditional dish for winter and festivals.
ranking.history: Cappelletti are a traditional pasta of the Romagna region of Italy; the name means 'little hats', from their resemblance to medieval hats. The 19th-century Italian gastronome Artusi recorded the method for cappelletti in his classic cookbook published in 1891. In San Marino and the Romagna region, cappelletti in broth are an essential dish of Christmas lunch, and households make them together before the holiday.

ranking.name: Passatelli
ranking.description: Breadcrumbs, Parmesan cheese, eggs, nutmeg and lemon zest are kneaded into a dough, pressed with a special tool into thick short noodles and cooked in broth.
ranking.history: Passatelli originated in the farmhouses of the Romagna region, where farmers invented the dish so as not to waste dry bread, embodying the rural wisdom of 'waste nothing'. Artusi's cookbook of 1891 also includes it. In San Marino and the Romagna region, it is a common noodle soup in winter and at festivals, especially around Easter.

ranking.name: Bustrengo
ranking.description: Breadcrumbs, cornmeal, honey, milk and eggs are mixed with dried fruits such as raisins, dried figs and apples and baked, giving a dense, moist texture, sweet with a fruity aroma.
ranking.history: Bustrengo is a traditional farmhouse dessert of San Marino and the Romagna region, which farmers made using leftover bread and seasonal fruit at home; it is a 'poor man's cake'. Because the ingredients are easy to get, in the past it was a dessert that every household made at Christmas and winter festivals, with each family's recipe differing slightly, and it remains one of San Marino's representative traditional desserts today.
